Industry observers note that to further assess the effects of EpTFIIAγ expression on carbon assimilation, we measured quantum yield of photosystem II photochemistry (ΦPSII). Transgenic EpTFIIAγ seedlings had approximately 14.6% higher ΦPSII than Fielder control plants under well-watered conditions, and approximately 29.9% greater ΦPSII under drought stress (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). These results suggested that EpTFIIAγ expression led to enhanced maintenance of PSII activity. EpTFIIAγ plants had improved light–response and CO2–response curves of net photosynthesis (Fig. 2b,c). In addition, the abundance of PSI, PSII, cytochrome b6/f and LHC proteins, as well as RuBisCO subunits were all increased in transgenic plants under well-watered or drought-stress conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5d). RuBisCO activity was increased in EpTFIIAγ plants (Extended Data Fig. 5c), which agreed with A–Ci curves showing higher maximum rates of RuBisCO carboxylation and electron transport (Extended Data Fig. 5e–h). Consistent with these increases, EpTFIIAγ leaves over-accumulated sucrose, glucose, starch and soluble sugars (Extended Data Fig. 5i), further demonstrating enhanced carbon assimilation in these plants. Of note, drought stress triggered a marked accumulation of root soluble sugars (for example, sucrose, glucose and fructose) in EpTFIIAγ plants compared with Fielder, whereas no such difference was observed under optimal conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5j), aligning with enhanced root growth under drought stress.

We next evaluated how EpTFIIAγ contributes to lifting photosynthetic capacity in field-grown plants. Chlorophyll content (soil and plant analyser development, SPAD), maximum quantum yield of PSII photochemistry (Fv/Fm) and photosynthetic rate were all enhanced in EpTFIIAγ transgenic plants in all five wheat cultivars compared with their corresponding wild-type controls at all of the tillering, stem elongation, flowering and milk development stages under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions (Fig. 2d–g and Supplementary Figs. 12–17). However, stomatal conductance and transpiration rate were lower in transgenic plants under water-limited conditions, although some EpTFIIAγ lines had slightly higher stomatal conductance under full-irrigation conditions. In agreement with these results, WUE (that is, the ratio of net photosynthetic rate to transpiration rate) was improved in EpTFIIAγ plants under water-limited conditions (Fig. 2d–g and Supplementary Figs. 14–17). Under full-irrigation field conditions, no obvious phenotypic changes in root development were seen between wild-type Fielder and transgenic plants. By contrast, all EpTFIIAγ lines had increased root length and biomass compared with Fielder under water-limited conditions (Fig. 2h–j), aligning with the stay-green phenotype observed in shoots (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9). Together, field-grown EpTFIIAγ wheat lines have enhanced WUE, resulting in slower water consumption, delayed senescence under water-limited conditions, and consequently more extensive root development, thereby facilitating greater water uptake. These data also suggested that enhanced photosynthetic capacity and CO2 assimilation contributed to the increased biomass and grain yield observed in EpTFIIAγ wheat plants.

Eukaryotic transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) requires numerous general transcription factors and cofactors to nucleate at core promoter sites, which typically contain several DNA sequence elements (for example, TATA boxes), to form the pre-initiation complex27. Among them, the transcription initiation factor TFIIA is a general cofactor that acts as an anti-repressor or co-activator27,28. In multicellular eukaryotes, the TFIIA complex typically comprises α-subunit, β-subunit and γ-subunit, encoded by TFIIAαβ and TFIIAγ genes27,29. To characterize the function of EpTFIIAγ, we first examined TFIIAγ sequences across species. EpTFIIAγ retains a conserved protein architecture while also harbouring a unique, lineage-specific N-terminal extension (Supplementary Table 7 and Supplementary Fig. 18). To determine whether EpTFIIAγ participates in transcription initiation, we first examined its subcellular localization in wheat protoplasts. EpTFIIAγ–GFP mainly localized to the nucleus, whereas intact TaTFIIAγ–GFP and AtTFIIAγ–GFP fusions revealed both nuclear and cytoplasmic localization (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). To investigate whether EpTFIIAγ could interact with endogenous TFIIAαβ to form the TFIIA holocomplex in plants, we conducted yeast two-hybrid, luciferase-complementation imaging and pulldown assays. These experiments consistently demonstrated that EpTFIIAγ fails to detectably interact with either wheat or Arabidopsis TFIIAαβ, whereas both TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ could interact with their corresponding TFIIAαβ proteins to form complete TFIIA complexes (Extended Data Fig. 6c–g). These results indicated that EpTFIIAγ does not appear to function as a transcription initiation factor in plants, or at least does so differently from these expression hosts.

The TFIIA recognition element (IIARE) located upstream of the TATA box enhances recruitment of TFIIA and other components to activate transcription at TATA-box promoter motifs27,29. We asked whether EpTFIIAγ could similarly bind to such recognition sites. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) indicated that MBP–EpTFIIAγ could indeed directly bind to an IIARE-containing TATA box, whereas neither wheat TaTFIIAγ nor Arabidopsis AtTFIIAγ displayed detectable binding (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i). Although fungal and plant TFIIAγ proteins share conserved α-helical and β-sheet architectures, EpTFIIAγ uniquely harbours an N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; Fig. 3a). Hypothesizing that this region may confer specialized biological function, we generated an IDR deletion variant (EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR)). This truncation did not bind to IIARE-containing TATA-box fragments, and likewise, its nuclear localization was impaired (Fig. 3b,c and Extended Data Fig. 6j). Conversely, fusing the EpTFIIAγ-derived IDR to TaTFIIAγ or AtTFIIAγ conferred binding to probes carrying an IIARE-containing TATA box (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 6j).

To test whether this IDR could drive liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), we expressed EpTFIIAγ–GFP in Nicotiana benthamiana leaf epidermal cells. Upon hyperosmotic stress, EpTFIIAγ maintained a homogeneous nuclear distribution and did not coalesce into condensates under either stress or non-stress conditions (Supplementary Fig. 19a). Moreover, His–EpTFIIAγ did not detectably form dynamic droplets in vitro, indicating that its relatively short IDR was insufficient to trigger LLPS (Supplementary Fig. 19b). Further evaluation of chromatin-binding dynamics through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy highlighted that EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR) exhibited markedly shallower bleach depth and accelerated recovery kinetics (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 19c–h), indicating attenuated chromatin association and higher mobility than full-length control. Stable-transgenic EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR) expression in wheat cv. Fielder conferred no obvious improvement in drought resistance relative to wild-type (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), indicating that the IDR is indeed indispensable for EpTFIIAγ function in the drought-stress response.

It has been revealed that to identify EpTFIIAγ-binding sites across the wheat genome, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) with transgenic plants stably expressing EpTFIIAγ–HA in the cv. Fielder (Fig. 3d). Across two replicates, 17,131 putative EpTFIIAγ-binding sites were identified, 85% of which are in intergenic regions and 15% in genic regions, including gene bodies as well as the 3-kb upstream and 300-bp downstream flanking sequences presumed to harbour the promoter and transcriptional terminator, respectively (Fig. 3e). Analysis of 2,570 genic binding sites identified 1,347 annotated genes bound by EpTFIIAγ–HA (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 8), and the core motif within these binding regions was enriched with a TATA-containing element (Fig. 3g). Gene Ontology analysis found that these EpTFIIAγ–HA target genes were enriched in terms related to stress responses, such as ‘transcriptional regulation’, ‘response to water deprivation’, ‘response to osmotic stress’, ‘response to cold’, ‘regulation of stomatal movement’ and ‘transpiration’; hormone responses, such as ‘response to abscisic acid (ABA)’, ‘response to auxin’ and ‘response to brassinosteroid’, as well as ‘photosynthesis’ and ‘chlorophyll biosynthesis’ (Fig. 3h). Further EMSAs confirmed that EpTFIIAγ could bind to promoter regions of 387 wheat genes, underscoring its capacity to regulate diverse biological pathways in planta, such as those related to stress response, development, photosynthesis and yield formation (Extended Data Fig. 7a, Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Fig. 20).

To define the regulatory network involved in the effects of EpTFIIAγ on photosynthetic efficiency, WUE and the drought-stress response, we compared transcriptomes of 20-day-old wild-type Fielder and EpTFIIAγ transgenic seedlings. This identified 1,953 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; fold change of more than 2 or less than 0.5, P < 0.05) in transgenic plants relative to Fielder, including 1,405 upregulated and 548 downregulated DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 7b–g and Supplementary Table 10). By examining overlap between ChIP–seq and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets, we identified 1,056 candidate target genes that are potentially bound and transcriptionally regulated by EpTFIIAγ, including 824 upregulated and 232 downregulated genes in EpTFIIAγ plants (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). Among them, stress-response-related genes involved in ABA and drought responses demonstrated strong enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 8c), such as wheat homologues of Arabidopsis MYBR1 (ref. 30), FBH4 (ref. 31) and DREB1C32 (Supplementary Tables 9 and 10). Other genes known to function in plant development, source–sink partitioning and grain yield were also present among upregulated DEGs, including the CONSTANS-like gene TaCol-B5 (ref. 33), wheat homologues of rice OsCIN2 (ref. 34) and OsSWEET4 (ref. 35), and homologues of Arabidopsis VND7 (ref. 36) and SWEET12 (ref. 37). Among photosynthesis-related DEGs, we found TaYCF9 and TaCP47, which are homologues of Arabidopsis PsbZ38 and CP47 (ref. 39) encoding subunits of the PSII reaction centre. In addition, we identified TaCOG1, a homologue of the Arabidopsis Dof transcription factor COG1, that promotes biomass accumulation by enhancing photosynthetic capacity40. TaGAPC1, a redox-dependent regulator of energy metabolism that mediates stress responses in Arabidopsis41, was also upregulated (Supplementary Tables 9 and 10).

MBP–EpTFIIAγ could bind in vitro to approximately 30-bp promoter fragments containing TATA motifs from TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1, and this interaction could be compromised by competition from unlabelled probes (Fig. 3i, Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Fig. 21a). ChIP–quantitative PCR (qPCR) indicated that these promoter fragments demonstrated greater enrichment in EpTFIIAγ–HA genomic DNA precipitated by anti-haemagglutinin antibody than by the immunoglobulin G (IgG) control (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 8e), demonstrating that EpTFIIAγ could indeed bind to TATA-containing core promoter motifs. In dual-luciferase reporter assays using approximately 1.5-kb promoter fragments, activities of target promoters were upregulated in the presence of EpTFIIAγ compared with empty vector controls (Fig. 3k, Extended Data Fig. 8f and Supplementary Fig. 21b), supported by real-time (RT)–qPCR analyses revealing that TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1 mRNAs were all expressed at higher levels in all three EpTFIIAγ transgenic lines than in wild-type Fielder (Extended Data Fig. 8g). These results collectively indicated that EpTFIIAγ functions as a transcriptional cofactor to regulate target gene expression.

To determine how downstream regulatory targets contribute to enhancing drought resistance, photosynthetic efficiency and grain yield in EpTFIIAγ plants, we generated transgenic wheat lines overexpressing TaDREB1C, TaCOG1 or TaCIN2 in the cv. Fielder background. TaDREB1C lines had enhanced drought resistance and WUE through accelerated stomatal closure and reduced transpiration compared with Fielder under drought stress (Extended Data Fig. 9a–g). This overexpression did not detectably alter growth period, which remained comparable with controls under full irrigation (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). Plants overexpressing TaCOG1 had enhanced photosynthetic and carbon-fixation capacities, resulting in increased biomass and grain yield relative to controls (Extended Data Fig. 9k–p). Moreover, TaCIN2 overexpression resulted in accelerated grain filling, ultimately increasing grain size and yield (Extended Data Fig. 9q–v). These results position the EpTFIIAγ regulon as pivotal for concurrently improving drought resilience and yield potential in wheat.

To investigate the mechanisms through which EpTFIIAγ drives enhanced drought resistance, photosynthetic capacity and grain yield, we conducted yeast two-hybrid screening using a cDNA library obtained from wheat cv. Chinese Spring seedlings. Four successive rounds of screening with EpTFIIAγ serving as bait yielded 112 candidate interacting proteins (Supplementary Table 11), including 22 putative transcription factors. After repeating yeast two-hybrid assays to confirm that EpTFIIAγ could interact with wheat homologues of Arabidopsis transcriptional activators WRKY46 (ref. 42), AKS1 (ref. 43), ARF6 (ref. 44) and VOZ1 (ref. 45) (Fig. 4a), luciferase-complementation imaging tested whether EpTFIIAγ could physically interact with these partners. Co-expression of EpTFIIAγ–C-terminal luciferase fragment (cLUC) with N-terminal luciferase fragment (nLUC)–TaWRKY46, nLUC–TaAKS1, nLUC–TaARF6 or nLUC–TaVOZ1 produced chemiluminescence, whereas no signal was observed in regions infiltrated with vector controls (Fig. 4b). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays further showed that co-expression of the EpTFIIAγ–cYFP with nYFP–TaWRKY46, nYFP–TaAKS1, nYFP–TaARF6 or nYFP–TaVOZ1 led to obvious YFP signal (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 22a,b). Pulldown assays indicated that MBP–EpTFIIAγ could interact with GST–TaWRKY46, GST–TaAKS1, GST–TaARF6 and HA–TaVOZ1 in vitro (Fig. 4d). Co-immunoprecipitation assays in N. benthamiana leaves co-expressing 35Spro:GFP–EpTFIIAγ and 35Spro:mCherry–TaWRKY46, 35Spro:mCherry–TaARF6 or 35Spro:mCherry–EpTFIIAγ with 35Spro:GFP–TaAKS1, 35Spro:GFP–TaVOZ1 also confirmed that EpTFIIAγ could physically interact with these transcription factors in planta (Fig. 4e). By contrast, the IDR-deleted EpTFIIAγ variant failed to detectably interact with any tested partners (Supplementary Fig. 22c,d), highlighting the essential role of this IDR. Moreover, no interactions were observed between wheat TaTFIIAγ and the transcription factors TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 or TaVOZ1 (Supplementary Fig. 22e,f), underscoring EpTFIIAγ functional specificity.

a, Yeast two-hybrid assays of EpTFIIAγ physical interactions with four wheat transcription factors. SD−T–L, SD medium without Trp and Leu; SD−T–L–H–A, SD medium without Trp, Leu, His and Ade. b, Luciferase complementation imaging of EpTFIIAγ interactions with the indicated wheat transcription factors. Recent findings suggest that to map genome-wide binding sites and target genes, we used CUT&Tag in stable-transgenic cv. Fielder plants expressing TaWRKY46–HA, TaAKS1–FLAG, TaARF6–HA or TaVOZ1–HA. Integrative analysis identified 467, 309, 495 and 505 target genes that are potentially co-bound and co-regulated by EpTFIIAγ with TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 or TaVOZ1, respectively (Supplementary Table 12 and Supplementary Fig. 23), suggesting direct involvement in the EpTFIIAγ regulatory network. GST–TaWRKY46 could bind in vitro to probes containing the W-box from the TaCol-B5, TaSWEET4 and TaSWEET12 promoters, and these binding events increased in the presence of MBP–EpTFIIAγ (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Similarly, GST–TaAKS1 could bind to probes harbouring the G-box or E-box from the TaDREB1C, TaCol-B5, TaYCF9 or TaCOG1 promoter regions, with the addition of MBP–EpTFIIAγ markedly strengthening these interactions in vitro. Moreover, GST–TaARF6 could interact with AuxRE-containing probes derived from the TaYCF9, TaFBH4 and TaCIN2 promoters, which was boosted by addition of MBP–EpTFIIAγ, whereas GST–TaVOZ1 bound to probes with a 5′-CTTCTT-3′ motif present in the TaCP47, TaVND7, TaMYBR1 and TaGAPC1 promoter regions, which also increased in the presence of MBP–EpTFIIAγ (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Dual-luciferase reporter assays indicated that TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 could activate genes with corresponding promoter recognition sites (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10b).

Sources indicate that to determine whether EpTFIIAγ functions coordinately with or independently of TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 in regulating target genes, we performed dual-luciferase reporter assays. Upon co-expressing EpTFIIAγ with each respective transcription factor, LUC activity driven by the TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1 promoters was greater than the expression of wheat transcription factors alone (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10b). To clarify whether activation of these transcription-factor genes contributed to the observed drought resistance of transgenic EpTFIIAγ plants, we examined drought resistance in lines overexpressing TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 (Extended Data Fig. 11a–d), as well as wrky46-knockout and arf6-knockout mutants by gene editing in cv. Fielder (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). All overexpression lines had enhanced drought resistance relative to Fielder, whereas both mutants had compromised drought resistance compared with Fielder controls (Extended Data Fig. 11g–j). To further characterize the genetic interactions of EpTFIIAγ with TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1, we crossed EpTFIIAγ plants (Fielder background) with each overexpression line. Under normal conditions, homozygous double-transgene-positive progeny of all crosses bore phenotypes comparable with that of TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 overexpression plants. By contrast, double-transgene-carrying hybrids revealed stronger drought resistance than control plants expressing a single transgene (Extended Data Fig. 11k,l). These findings collectively demonstrated that EpTFIIAγ physically interacts with select transcription activators, such as TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 or TaVOZ1, and that their interactions resulted in additive effects on EpTFIIAγ target gene expression, consequently enhancing the drought response, photosynthesis and grain yield.

Sources indicate that performance of EpTFIIAγ rice and maize lines was tested in the field over multiple seasons. Two-year evaluation (2023 and 2024) of rice in Hanzhong (Shaanxi Province) found that plant height, grain yield per plant, grain size (ratio of grain length to width) and 1,000-grain weight were all increased in the transgenic lines compared with wild-type controls under full-irrigation conditions, and this difference was more pronounced under water deficit (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 12c,e). EpTFIIAγ rice had 10.2–11.9% increases in grain yield per plant under full irrigation and 19.7–24.1% increases under water-deficit conditions relative to wild-type Nipponbare. EpTFIIAγ maize was examined over 3-year (2023–2025) field trials in Zhangye (Gansu Province), Changji and Aksu (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region), which are arid regions and notable maize production areas (Supplementary Fig. 5). All EpTFIIAγ maize lines were taller than wild-type B73 under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions, although grain number per ear, yield per plant and 100-grain weight were only increased under water-limited conditions (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12d,f,g). Grain yield per plant increased by a striking 27.9–37.2% in Zhangye (Extended Data Fig. 12f), 31.9–42.4% in Changji (Fig. 5h) and 31.1–35.4% in Aksu (Extended Data Fig. 12g) under water-limited conditions. Although growth duration of EpTFIIAγ plants remained comparable with that of wild-type controls under full irrigation, drought stress was accompanied by a 3–5-day delay in rice maturation and 2–4-day longer time to maturity in maize (Extended Data Fig. 12h,i). These cumulative results indicated that transgenic expression of EpTFIIAγ consistently and substantially improved drought resistance and yield of major cereal crops.

Sources indicate that using multifunctional, pleiotropic genes to simultaneously modulate multiple pathways could potentially streamline genetic improvement efforts aimed at enhancing crop stress resistance and yield16,46. Here we demonstrate that transgenic expression of EpTFIIAγ synergistically enhances both drought resistance and yield in cereal crops. In field trials, transgenic wheat and rice expressing EpTFIIAγ had greater yield and biomass production than respective wild-type controls across full water availability and water-deficit conditions (Fig. 5g, Extended Data Fig. 12e and Supplementary Fig. 7). In maize, these benefits were exclusively observed under water-deficit conditions (Fig. 5h and Extended Data Fig. 12f,g), whereas the lack of a yield response under well-watered conditions could potentially reflect functional redundancy in regulating grain production in C4 species with high metabolic efficiency and strict constraints on reproductive synchrony47,48. Plants expressing EpTFIIAγ consistently showed higher drought resistance and grain yield than wild-type counterparts across different genetic backgrounds and cultivars (Fig. 1, Supplementary Tables 1–6 and Supplementary Figs. 6 and 7). Moreover, EpTFIIAγ expression also confers resistance to other major stressors, including excessive heat, lodging and stripe rust (Extended Data Fig. 2), indicating that the inverse relationship between stress resistance and yield can be decoupled or even reversed.

In a recent development, although used as a transgene expressed in cereal crops, EpTFIIAγ was isolated from E. pusillum, an extremophile fungus adapted to drought-prone conditions24. The N-terminal IDR of EpTFIIAγ endows it with unique functions in plants, enabling binding to TATA-box-containing motifs and physical interactions with endogenous transcriptional activators (Figs. 3a,b and 4a–e and Supplementary Fig. 22). By contrast, plant TFIIAγ homologues are restricted to basal transcriptional initiation and do not appear to mediate drought responses (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 6). IDRs are known to mediate LLPS49, yet EpTFIIAγ did not detectably undergo LLPS (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 19). Instead, its IDR is thought to undergo transient, weak DNA interactions that emerge as precise localization patterns on chromatin50,51. This mechanism allows EpTFIIAγ to integrate into the plant regulatory network for coordinately targeting pathways involved in transcriptional regulation, stress and hormone responses, transpiration, photosynthesis, chlorophyll biosynthesis, sugar transport and grain filling, ultimately enhancing drought resistance and grain yield under greenhouse and field conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Fig. 24).

In a recent development, crucially, enhanced photosynthesis in flag leaves and grain starch accumulation under well-watered conditions, together with a slightly longer growth cycle under drought, suggest that EpTFIIAγ improves yield by increasing source-to-sink transport of photoassimilates, thereby promoting starch biosynthesis during the 5–15-day period after pollination (Fig. 2, Extended Data Figs. 3–5 and Supplementary Figs. 7f,l and 12–17). Improved carbon assimilation in EpTFIIAγ plants did not promote root development under well-watered conditions, but did lead to enhanced root growth under drought stress (Fig. 2h–j). In this context, we propose that excess photoassimilates are preferentially allocated to aboveground biomass under non-limiting water conditions, whereas drought stress triggers ABA signalling to redirect carbon flux towards the roots to enhance water absorption and retention37. Several lines of evidence support the hypothesis that EpTFIIAγ confers drought resistance and yield enhancement in wheat through the following pathways: (1) ameliorating drought resistance and WUE through TaDREB1C; (2) boosting photosynthesis, biomass and grain yield through TaCOG1 and TaCol-B5; (3) enhancing photosynthetic assimilation and grain filling through TaCIN2; and (4) interacting with several transcriptional activators to enhance the expression of target genes (Fig. 4, Extended Data Figs. 9–11 and Supplementary Fig. 23). These synergistic effects reproducibly conferred enhanced plant fitness and yield for all three cereal crops. Next steps include introducing EpTFIIAγ into contemporary, farmer-preferred rice cultivars and elite maize hybrid backgrounds, as well as exploring functionality in other staple crops not adapted to drought.

Recent findings suggest that heterologous expression of other extremophile transgenes can also improve resistance to abiotic stressors in Arabidopsis or tobacco, such as EpANN from E. pusillum52, versatile peroxidase from Bjerkandera adusta53 and hsp70/Thkel1 from Trichoderma harzianum54. However, whether these genes can improve stress resistance in cereals has not been reported, and mechanisms for regulating resistance remain poorly understood. Given the restrictions on transgenic plants in some growing regions, it may be possible to enhance crop drought resilience without genetic modification by targeting pathways controlled by EpTFIIAγ through chemical or biological strategies. For example, certain ABA receptor agonists can mimic ABA signalling to trigger stomatal closure and stress responses55,56,57. A photoactivatable T6P precursor overcomes source and sink limitations under diverse conditions, boosting wheat yields by 5–17%8. Certain symbiotic fungi (for example, Trichoderma) secrete metabolites that can induce systemic drought resistance58,59,60. Although these strategies circumvent certain biosafety concerns associated with transgenics, their transient and environment-dependent efficacy potentially increases long-term costs. Transgenic approaches provide durable and heritable resistance, thereby lowering costs. In agricultural practice, combining genetic engineering with certain chemical and/or biological treatments may lead to synergistic improvements in yield and stress mitigation.

It has been revealed that despite these advances, solutions remain urgently needed to overcome obstacles of diminishing arable land and intensifying climate change while doubling global food production by 2050. This study demonstrates the potential to substantially improve yields among the major staple crops, despite centuries of previous breeding efforts, at least in countries where genetically modified plants can be grown. Beyond demonstrating that EpTFIIAγ can dramatically boost productivity by enhancing drought resistance and grain yield, our study unveils a conserved mechanism for orchestrating stress responses, development, photosynthesis and yield to ultimately decouple antagonistic regulatory pathways. These findings open newly introduced avenues for engineering plant growth and stress resilience by key factors such as EpTFIIAγ.

Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) plants were grown under both controlled environments or field conditions. For controlled environments, wheat seeds were immersed in a 70% (v/v) ethanol for 2 min. Afterwards, the seeds were rinsed three times with sterile distilled water to remove any residual ethanol. The surface-sterilized seeds were then stratified at 4 °C in darkness for 3 days, followed by germination under white light (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance) at room temperature. Germinated seedlings were planted in a mixture of nutrient soil and vermiculite (3:1) and maintained in a controlled growth chamber (LRX-2000D-LED, Ningbo Prandt Instrument) under 200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 14 °C and 12 °C day and night temperature cycle with 60% humidity. Field trials were conducted in China with uniform wheat seeds sown at a daily average temperature of 15–20 °C (usually in October). Detailed information for each experimental site is provided in Supplementary Fig. 5. Specifically, EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat and wild-type controls were planted in Yangling (Shaanxi Province, 34° 16′ N, 108° 04′ E) during 2023–2025, and three other arid regions with an annual rainfall of 120–250 mm in 2025, including Heyang (Shaanxi Province, 35° 43′ N, 110° 02′ E), Cangzhou (Hebei Province, 38° 33′ N, 116° 38′ E) and Linfen (Shanxi Province, 36° 56′ N, 112° 34′ E). In each experimental field, basal fertilizers were applied at a rate of 37,500–45,000 kg ha–1 decomposed organic fertilizer, 600–750 kg ha–1 compound fertilizer with 1:1:1 of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), 22.5 kg ha–1 zinc sulfate and 7.5 kg ha–1 borax. All fertilizers were thoroughly mixed and incorporated into the soil during plowing to ensure uniform distribution in the plow layer. At the Yangling site, full-irrigation and water-limited growth conditions were established, with the water-limited condition implemented using a rain-out shelter and controlled irrigation. After initial irrigation at sowing by a drip irrigation system, water-limited plots received approximately 30% of the water volume supplied to full-irrigation plots for the rest of the growing season. At the other sites, local wheat production management was applied after an initial thorough watering at sowing.

Phenotypic characterization of rice (O. sativa) was conducted at the seedling stage under controlled conditions and at the mature stage under field conditions. For seedling-stage assessment, seeds were surface sterilized using a 10% (v/v) sodium hypochlorite solution and incubated in darkness at 37 °C for 3 days, followed by germination under white light (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance). Germinated seeds were transplanted into a mixture of Pindstrup turf and vermiculite (1:1) and cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance, 14-h light and 10-h dark photoperiod, 28 °C and 26 °C day and night temperature cycle and 60% humidity. For scoring at the maturity stage under field conditions, seedlings with healthy and uniform appearance were transplanted into paddy fields in Hanzhong (Shaanxi Province, 33.04° N, 107.01° E) in early June. Basal fertilizer was applied at 30,000 kg ha–1 decomposed farmyard manure, 450 kg ha–1 ammonium bicarbonate, 225 kg ha–1 potassium chloride and 375 kg ha–1 superphosphate. The field was rotavated to mix the fertilizer evenly with the soil, then flooded to maintain a 3–5-cm water layer. Transplanting followed a spacing regime of 30 cm between rows; each transgenic line and control were planted in five rows with ten plants per row and 20 cm between individual seedlings. Within 7 days post-transplanting, a 3–5-cm shallow water layer was maintained to promote seedling recovery. From the end of seedling recovery to the tillering stage, the water layer was adjusted to 2–3 cm. From the booting stage to ripening, a 3–4-cm shallow water layer was retained until rice maturity. Drought-stress treatment was applied by halting irrigation and draining standing water at the booting stage (panicle elongation). Irrigation was resumed to allow recovery after irreversible leaf-rolling symptoms were observed for 5 consecutive days in the experimental group. For each genotype, at least three biological replicates were grown under each treatment condition.

It has been revealed that cultivation and propagation of maize (Z. mays) were carried out in field plots at Northwest A&F University (Yangling, 34° 16′ N, 108° 04′ E) during 2021–2022, and self-pollination was performed to obtain homozygous lines. For seedling-stage experiments under controlled conditions, seeds were sown in nursery pots filled with a 3:1 mixture of nutrient soil and vermiculite, and cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m–2 s–1 irradiance, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 25 °C and 23 °C day and night temperature cycle and 60% relative humidity. For phenotyping at the maturity stage under field conditions, plants were in experimental fields in Zhangye (Gansu Province, 38.56° N, 100.26° E) from May–September in 2023, Changji (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, 43.06° N, 86.18° E) from May–September in 2024 and Aksu (Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, 41.71° N, 80.81° E) from May–September in 2025. Maize lines were sown in accordance with the local cropping season, maintaining uniformity in planting density, irrigation, fertilizer application and pest control treatments. Each genotype had four replicate plots (4 rows × 13 seeds) under full-irrigation and drought treatments, respectively. To mitigate border effects, each plot was surrounded by dedicated buffer rows, thereby ensuring uniform conditions among plants used for data collection. Drought treatment was imposed from the V5 stage (fifth leaf with visible ligule) until completion of silking, during which the soil water potential gradually decreased from −20 to −220 kPa. Watering was typically applied using a drip irrigation system at approximately 10-day intervals, with drought-treated plots receiving approximately 40% of the water volume supplied to well-watered controls. Buried Watermark 200SS sensors were used to monitor and maintain soil water potential (0 to −20 kPa) in plots treated with full irrigation. Following harvest, dried ears were assessed for yield per plant and kernels per ear.

Industry observers note that to generate transgenic lines either heterologously expressing EpTFIIAγ or overexpressing TaTFIIAγ, TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaWRKY46, TaVOZ1, TaDREB1C, TaCOG1 and TaCIN2 in wheat, respective coding sequences were cloned into the pCAMBIA3301 vector under the control of the Ubiquitin promoter and NOS terminator. For CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing of TaARF6 and TaWRKY46, single guide RNAs targeting exons were designed using E-CRISP (http://www.e-crisp.org/), cloned into the pBUE411 vector via BsaI restriction sites, and verified by Sanger sequencing25. Constructs were then introduced into Agrobacterium tumefaciens EHA105 and transformed into immature embryos of wheat cvs. Fielder, XN979, XN511, JM22 and XZ9104 following established protocols61. Transgenic T0 plants were identified by PCR and transgene expression was confirmed either by RT–qPCR or by western blotting. Positive T0 plants were propagated to the T2 or T3 generation in a greenhouse for subsequent phenotyping and trait scoring. Primers used are provided in the Supplementary Table 15 and antibodies are described below.

Nipponbare transformation, the EpTFIIAγ coding region was cloned into the pBWA(V)HS vector under the control of the Cauliflower Mosaic Virus 35S (CaMV 35S) promoter and CaMV 35S-polyA terminator. The construct was introduced into A. tumefaciens EHA105, and transformation into immature embryos of Nipponbare. Transgenic T0 plants were identified by PCR, and transgene expression was confirmed by either RT–qPCR or western blotting. Positive T0 plants were propagated to the T3 generation in a greenhouse for subsequent phenotyping and trait scoring.

Industry observers note that for Z. mays inbred line B73 transformation, the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pBCXUN vector48 under the control of the maize Ubiquitin promoter and NOS terminator. For generation of transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana in the Col-0 background, the full-length coding regions of EpTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were cloned into the pGreen-0029 vector62 under the CaMV 35S promoter and NOS terminator, introduced into A. tumefaciens GV3101, and transformed using the floral-dip method63. T1 seeds were screened on half-strength Murashige and Skoog (1/2 MS) medium with 50 mg l−1 kanamycin, and homozygous T3 lines were used for phenotypic analysis.

It has been revealed that for wheat, seeds from wild-type and three T3 transgenic lines were sown side by side in nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture in plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height), and cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity for approximately 30 days. Drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days until the soil volumetric water content reached approximately 3% and was maintained at this level for an additional 5 days. Survival rates were assessed 3 days after rewatering by scoring all plants with green and viable leaves. At least 16 plants per genotype were analysed across three or four biological replicates.

For rice, Nipponbare controls and T3 transgenic seeds were germinated in darkness at 37 °C for 3 days, and subsequently transferred to white light. Germinated seeds were then planted side by side in a mixture of Pindstrup turf and vermiculite (1:1, w/w) in plastic boxes (35 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm, length × width × height), and cultivated in a growth chamber under the same growth conditions as wheat, but with a 28 °C and 26 °C day and night temperature cycle. After approximately 30 days of growth, drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 21 days until the soil volumetric water content reached approximately 3%, then maintaining this level for an additional 5 days. To assess stress resistance, survival rates were recorded 3 days after rewatering by scoring all plants with green, viable leaves. At least 16 plants per line were analysed across three biological replicates.

Recent findings suggest that for maize, wild-type B73 and three independent T3 transgenic lines were grown side by side in boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height) filled with a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture. After germination, seedlings were cultivated under the same environmental conditions as wheat, except using a 25 °C and 23 °C day and night temperature regime. At the three-leaf stage, drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days, followed by rewatering. Survival rates were assessed 7 days later by scoring all plants with green and viable leaves. At least 16 plants per line were analysed across three biological replicates.

Sources indicate that for Arabidopsis, surface-sterilized seeds were sown on half-strength MS medium, stratified in the dark at 4 °C for 3 days, and then transferred to a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 22 °C and 20 °C day and night temperature cycle, 60% humidity and a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod.
