Seeds of EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants and wild-type controls were sown in 7 cm × 10 cm pots containing a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture and grown in a growth chamber. At the three-leaf stage, seedlings were exposed to 42 °C for 36 h and allowed to recover at 23 °C for 4 days. Seedling survival rates were calculated based on the number of individual plants with green, viable shoots. At least nine seedlings per genotype were analysed per assay, with three independent experiments. Maximum photochemical efficiency of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) was measured using a FluorPen FP110 fluorometer (PSI). Electrolyte leakage was determined using a conductivity meter (DDSJ-307F, Shanghai INESA Scientific Instruments). Relative electrolyte conductivity (%) was calculated as (C1 – C0)/(C2 – C0) × 100%, where C1 represents initial conductivity before boiling, C2 is the final conductivity after boiling and C0 is the conductivity of deionized water.

Recent findings suggest that wild-type Fielder and EpTFIIAγ transgenic wheat plants were cultivated in a growth chamber under 200 μmol photons m−2 s−1, 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Three-week-old seedlings were inoculated with Pst urediniospores and maintained in darkness at 12 °C and 100% relative humidity for 24 h, after which plants were returned to standard growth conditions. Disease phenotypes were evaluated following the development of stripe rust symptoms. Relative fungal biomass was quantified by qPCR analysis of the ratio of Pst-specific PstEF transcripts relative to that of the wheat reference gene, TaEF64, in CTAB-extracted genomic DNA.

For histological analyses, reactive oxygen species accumulation was visualized by staining infected leaves with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (1 mg ml−1). Stained samples were examined using a BX-51 microscope (Olympus). Stomata associated with haustorial mother-cell formation were defined as successful infection sites, and the 3,3′-diaminobenzidine-stained area at each site was quantified using CellSens Entry software (Olympus). At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point. Fungal infection structures were visualized by WGA–Alexa Fluor 488 staining (20 μg ml−1; Amresco) following tissue clearing and alkali treatment. Samples were mounted in 50% glycerol and examined using an Olympus BX-53 fluorescence microscope equipped with a GFP filter set. Substomatal vesicles, infection hyphae and other fungal structures were observed, and hyphal length and fungal colonization area were quantified using CellSens Entry software. At least 30 infection sites were analysed for each time point.

Wheat drought resistance at the maturity stage was evaluated under full-irrigation (that is, control) and water-limited conditions in the field. Each plot measured 5 m × 2 m and consisted of 25 rows, with 20-cm spacing between rows and 10 cm between plants. Control plots were irrigated regularly throughout the entire growing season, and water-limited plots were isolated using a 1.5-m-deep underground waterproof barrier and covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation. After the initial irrigation at sowing, water-limited plots received approximately 30% of the water volume applied to the well-watered plots for the remainder of the season.

It has been revealed that photosynthetic parameters of wheat were recorded with a LI-6400XT portable photosynthesis system (LI-COR) at four Zadoks growth stages from tillering (Z25) to milk development (Z75). Net photosynthesis rate (Pn), transpiration rate (Tr), stomatal conductance (Gs) and instantaneous water use efficiency (calculated as Pn/Tr) were measured from at least 15 plants per line. Light-response and CO2-response curves were fitted using the Farquhar–von Caemmerer–Berry model to estimate maximum carboxylation rate (Vcmax) and maximum electron transport rate (Jmax). Chlorophyll fluorescence (Fv/Fm) and SPAD values were measured using a hand-held chlorophyll-fluorescence measurement instrument (FluorPen FP 110, FluorCam) and chlorophyll meter (SPAD-502, Konica Minolta), respectively. Leaf area of the main tiller was measured using a leaf-area meter (Yaxin-1242, Dianjiang Technology). Agronomic traits, including plant height, spike number, spike length, spikelet number, grain number per spike, grain length, grain width, 1,000-grain weight, yield per plant, biomass and harvest index were measured from 50–100 plants per line. Grains were oven-dried at 37 °C before yield quantification.

Rice agronomic traits were evaluated in the field at maturity. Seeds were sown in a seedling nursery and transplanted into the field at 25 days after sowing. A wide–narrow row-planting pattern was adopted in the field, with 5 rows × 10 plants per plot. Each line was randomly assigned to three plots (that is, three biological replicates). Water-limited plots were covered with a rain-out shelter to exclude natural precipitation, and drought stress was initiated at booting stage by withholding irrigation and opening drainage valves to remove standing water. Drought treatment was terminated and followed by a rewatering recovery phase once either the experimental or control plants showed irreversible leaf-rolling symptoms that persisted for 5 consecutive days. At maturity, each plant was harvested individually. Traits assessed included plant height, grain size, 1,000-grain weight and grain yield per plant.

According to recent reports, maize field trials were conducted at the three abovementioned locations under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions. Drought treatment was applied through artificial irrigation control using a drip irrigation system equipped with underground Watermark 200SS sensors to monitor and maintain soil water potential. Each treatment included four replicate plots (2.6 m wide; 0.4 m row spacing), with four rows per line. Agronomic traits, including plant height, grain number per ear, yield per plant and 100-grain weight, were measured following open pollination.

Wheat lodging resistance was evaluated using the second basal internode of the main tiller. Stem breaking strength was measured at 10 days after anthesis using a plant stem strength tester (IN-JG2, Shandong Holder Electronic Technology). Stem diameter was measured on the same internode using a digital caliper. Each stem was measured three times, and 20 biological replicates were analysed for each genotype.

For stem histology, the middle region of the peduncle internode was collected at 15 days post-anthesis and fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and clearing in xylene, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections (6–8 μm) were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems) and subjected to safranin–fast green double staining. In brief, sections were stained with safranin, differentiated in 90% ethanol, counterstained with fast green, cleared in a 1:1 (v/v) xylene–ethanol mixture and mounted. Panoramic images were acquired using SlideViewer software (v2.9.0), and stem diameter, vascular bundle number and mechanical tissue thickness were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

For seedling-stage stress experiments, germinated wheat seedlings were grown in 7 cm × 7 cm × 10 cm pots with Hoagland’s modified nutrient solution for 3 days under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod at 14 °C and 12 °C (day and night) with 60% relative humidity. Subsequently, the control group was continuously cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution, whereas the drought-stress group was cultured in modified Hoagland’s nutrient solution containing 20% (w/v) PEG6000. Seedlings in both groups were grown for 3–4 weeks, with the culture solution replaced every 3 days, after which root parameters were scored. The root system of each seedling was excised, lateral roots were separated from nodes, evenly spread in a transparent plastic tray with 0.5 cm of deionized water, and intertwined fine lateral branches were gently separated with forceps to avoid overlap. Primary root length, root fresh weight and root dry weight were measured manually.

Sources indicate that wheat plants were grown in PVC columns (150 cm × 15 cm) filled with soil under well-watered and water-limited (water supply terminated at the jointing stage) conditions, with one plant per column. When wheat reached the grain-filling stage, the soil and root system were carefully removed from the columns. Roots were rinsed with running water to remove adhering soil and impurities, then excised from shoots. Root length was measured immediately after cleaning. Subsequently, roots were placed in paper envelopes and dried in a forced-air drying oven at 65 °C for 7 days, after which root dry weight was determined.

Water loss assays were performed on 4-week-old wheat seedlings as previously described25. Fully expanded third leaves were excised and immediately weighed to record their initial fresh weight (FW0). Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper under ambient room conditions (22–25 °C, 40–60% relative humidity, with light exposure) without covering. Fresh weight (FWt) was recorded at regular intervals. Water loss was expressed as a percentage of the initial fresh weight using the formula: Water loss rate (%) = [(FW0 − FWt)/FW0] × 100. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Water loss assays on Arabidopsis were carried out as previously described65. In brief, fully expanded rosette leaves from 3-week-old plants were detached at the same time of day to minimize circadian effects. The initial fresh weight (FW0) was recorded immediately using a precision analytical balance. Leaves were then placed on dry filter paper in a controlled environment (22 °C, 50–60% relative humidity, no direct airflow). Fresh weights (FWt) were measured at specified time intervals, typically every 30 or 60 min for 6 h. Water loss rate was calculated using the same formula as for wheat. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Infrared thermography was performed on 4-week-old greenhouse-grown seedlings that were subjected to 15 days of water withholding, during which soil water content was maintained at approximately 50% of well-watered capacity. Leaf surface temperatures under different treatments were recorded using a FLIR A655sc infrared camera (Teledyne FLIR). Thermal images were analysed using FLIR ResearchIR Max (v4.40) to quantify temperature differences and assess drought-induced physiological responses.

To evaluate photosynthesis-related changes, multispectral imaging was conducted using the PhenoBox live-plant multispectral imaging analysis system (LemnaTec GmbH). Five-leaf-stage wheat seedlings were individually cultivated in plots filled with nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture under controlled growth-chamber conditions. Imaging was performed under three distinct soil-moisture regimes, including well watered (soil water content maintained at approximately 90%), mild drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 50%) and severe drought (soil water content reduced to approximately 30%). Four surface multispectral images were captured for each plant. Standardized imaging protocols were applied to ensure consistent lighting and sensor calibration. Two spectral values, normalized water index and normalized difference vegetation index, were used to assess plant water status and physiological responses under drought stress: normalized water index = (R970 – R850)/(R970 + R850) and normalized difference vegetation index = (R800 – R670)/(R800 + R670), with R representing reflectance and numbers referring to wavelength (nm).

For chlorophyll fluorescence measurements, imaging was performed using the live-plant imaging system CV-200 produced by Beijing Feizhi Technology and controlled by CropVision_Controller_v2 software. Fluorescence images were captured under stable-lighting conditions at the same time points used for multispectral imaging. The effective ΦPSII was automatically extracted using the software and was used to evaluate photosynthetic performance and drought-stress responses in wheat seedlings across the different water treatments.

Stomatal density measurements were performed following a published protocol66. To determine stomatal density in wheat, the middle region of the abaxial surface of the fully expanded second leaf of seedlings was selected for analysis. The abaxial epidermis was carefully adhered to a piece of transparent adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll tissue were then gently scraped off using a razor blade. The tape carrying the intact abaxial epidermal cells was subsequently mounted on a standard microscope slide (75 mm × 25 mm) for microscopic observation. A minimum of ten slides were prepared for each wheat line. Stomata were observed and photographed using compound microscope (Olympus IX71) under a ×10 objective lens, and stomatal density was calculated as the number of stomata per unit area of the field of view.

Recent findings suggest that for Arabidopsis, fully expanded and healthy functional leaves (typically the fifth or sixth true leaf) were selected. The abaxial surface of each leaf was gently pressed onto clear adhesive tape. The upper epidermis and mesophyll were carefully removed using a razor blade, leaving the lower epidermis adhered to the tape. The tape carrying the epidermal imprint was then mounted smoothly onto a standard glass slide (75 mm × 25 mm), avoiding air bubbles. At least ten slides were prepared per line for analysis.

Stomatal aperture measurements in wheat and Arabidopsis were determined following established protocols65. For wheat, a fully expanded second leaf was excised and incubated in stomatal opening buffer containing 0.05 M KNO3, 10 mM MES and 50 μM CaCl2 (pH 6.15) under light conditions (200 μmol photons m–2 s–1, 25 °C) for 1.5 h or in darkness for 1 h. Leaves were then exposed to drought treatment under ambient air for 10 min, followed by incubation in continuous light, continuous dark or a light-to-dark transition for 30 min. The abaxial surface was carefully blot dried and adhered to transparent tape, and the adaxial epidermis and mesophyll cells were gently removed using a razor blade. The exposed abaxial epidermal layer on the tape was then mounted on a microscope slide for imaging. For Arabidopsis, the fifth or sixth rosette leaves were harvested and incubated in MES buffer (10 mM MES-KOH, pH 6.15, 10 mM KCl and 50 μM CaCl2) in a light incubator for 2.5 h to induce stomatal opening. The leaves were subsequently transferred to MES buffer containing 20% w/v PEG6000 and incubated for 2 h. Epidermal strips were prepared and imaged using a compound microscope (Olympus IX71). Stomatal aperture was defined as the width of the pore between the two guard cells, and the stomatal aperture ratio (width:length) was measured using ImageJ (v1.8.0). Data for each ecotype were collected from a minimum of 100 stomata.

It has been revealed that wheat seedlings were grown under controlled conditions until the three-leaf stage. Once soil moisture content declined below 30%, leaf samples were collected at designated intervals. Each genotype comprised three biological replicates, with each sample weighing no less than 1.5 g. Samples were placed in dry envelopes and dried in a constant-temperature forced-air oven at 60 °C until completely desiccated. The dried tissue was then ground into a fine powder for carbon isotope analysis using the stable-isotope ratio mass spectrometry method. Ground samples were treated with 4 mol dm−3 HCl for 24 h, then washed with deionized water until neutral, dried, ground and sieved through a 60-mesh screen. Approximately 0.4 mg of the solid sample was accurately weighed, placed into a tin cup and hermetically sealed, and placed in a 96-well plate. Isotopic measurements were conducted using a Flash 1112 Elemental Analyzer coupled to a Delta V Plus Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Finnigan). The carbon isotope ratio (δ13C) was calculated relative to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) international standard using the formula: δ13C (‰) = [(Rsample/RVPDB) – 1] × 1,000, where R is the ratio of 13C to 12C. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

Uniform wheat seeds were germinated at room temperature for 3 days and subsequently grown in half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution for 1 week. Seedlings were then subjected to either control conditions or drought stress induced by 15% (w/v) PEG6000. After 10 days of treatment, leaf and root tissues were harvested, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Three independent biological replicates were collected for each treatment. Hormone quantification was performed by Metware Biotechnology using an AB Sciex QTRAP 6500 LC–MS/MS system.

Wheat seeds were sown side by side in plastic boxes (32 cm × 24 cm × 12 cm, length × width × height) filled with a nutrient soil:vermiculite (3:1, w/w) mixture. Seedlings were cultured under a 16-h light and 8-h dark photoperiod, 14 °C and 12 °C day and night temperature and 60% relative humidity for approximately 30 days (three-leaf stage). Drought stress was imposed by withholding water for approximately 20 days until leaf wilting was observed. Leaves were collected from at least three individual plants under well-watered and drought-stressed conditions. The activity of RuBisCO, along with the contents of chlorophyll, soluble sugars, sucrose, glucose and starch were measured using commercial assay kits all obtained from Solarbio: BC0445 for RuBisCO activity, BC0995 for chlorophyll, BC2460 for sucrose, BC0030 for soluble sugars, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch, all following the manufacturer’s instructions. At least three biological replicates were used for each genotype or treatment.

To evaluate wheat grain development and filling dynamics, main tiller spikes were tagged before anthesis. Under both full-irrigation and water-limited conditions, grains from the six central spikelets of each tagged spike were sampled at 5-day intervals from anthesis to physiological maturity, with a minimum of nine spikes collected per genotype per time point. Grain length, width and thickness were measured in 60–100 grains with a digital caliper (0.01-mm resolution); fresh weight was determined for 100-grain samples. Dry weight was obtained by drying samples at 80 °C to a constant weight following a 30-min pre-treatment at 105 °C. The mean grain-filling rate was calculated as the final grain dry weight divided by the grain-filling duration, expressed as mg per grain per day.

In a recent development, flag leaf sheaths and developing grains were harvested at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 days after flowering. Soluble sugars (sucrose, fructose and glucose) and starch contents were quantified using commercial assay kits from Solarbio (BC2460 for sucrose, BC6360 for fructose, BC2500 for glucose and BC0700 for starch). Enzymatic activity assays were conducted using kits for sucrose synthase (SUS; BC0585), cell-wall invertase (CWI; BC4325) and ADP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (AGPase; BC0435) following the manufacturer’s protocols. All assays were performed with at least three independent biological replicates.

For grain histology, developing grains were collected from central spikelets at 15 days after flowering, then fixed in formalin alcohol acetate solution (G2355, Solarbio) at 23 °C for 48 h. Following dehydration through a graded ethanol series (75–100%, v/v) and xylene clearing, samples were embedded in paraffin. Sections of 6–8 μm thickness were cut using a rotary microtome (Leica RM2235; Leica Biosystems). For histological analysis, sections were stained with toluidine blue, whereas starch granules were visualized using periodic acid–Schiff reagent. Images were acquired using SlideViewer panoramic scanning software (v2.9.0). Grain cell size, cell number and starch granule number were quantified using ImageJ (v1.53).

Industry observers note that total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. First-strand complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 1 μg of DNase-treated RNA using the HiScript reverse transcription kit (R223-01, Vazyme). RT–qPCR was performed in a 20-μl reaction volume containing 1.4 μl cDNA (pre-diluted to a concentration of 200 ng μl−1), 0.4 μM primers and 10 μl of SYBR Green Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme), using a CFX96 real-time PCR system (Bio-Rad). Gene-expression levels were calculated using the \({2}^{-\Delta \Delta {{\rm{C}}}_{{\rm{T}}}}\) method67 with TaActin1 (TraesCS1B01G283900) serving as the reference gene for normalization. Primer sequences used for RT–qPCR are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

Sources indicate that the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Δhog1 mutant, which is sensitive to osmotic stress and lacks a functional copy of a gene encoding a high osmolarity glycerol 1 protein kinase (HOG1)68, was used to assess the drought-resistance function of TFIIAγ proteins. Coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were amplified via PCR using primers with flanking attB sites. These fragments were first cloned into the pDONR221 entry vector (Invitrogen) via BP recombination using the Gateway cloning system and subsequently transferred into the pGAD426 destination vector (Addgene) through an LR (attL and attR) recombination reaction. Recombinant plasmids were transformed into Δhog1 cells using the Frozen-EZ Yeast Transformation Kit (Zymo Research). Transformed strains were selected on synthetic dropout medium lacking uracil (SD−Ura). The pGAD426-GUS plasmid was used as a control.

For stress-tolerance assays, 10 μl of yeast culture (OD600 nm = 0.6) was spotted onto SD−Ura solid medium supplemented with 0.75 M sorbitol and incubated at 28 °C for 3 days. Growth in SD−Ura liquid medium containing 0.75 M sorbitol was monitored by measuring OD600 nm at 24-h intervals.

Industry observers note that the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ (excluding translational stop codons) were cloned in-frame into the N-terminal region of the pJIT163-GFP expression vectors64, both driven by the CaMV 35S promoter. The resulting fusion constructs were introduced into wheat protoplasts (pJIT163-TFIIAγ-GFP). Transformed wheat protoplasts were incubated for 16 h to permit transient expression. GFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and an emission wavelength range of 500–530 nm. Nuclei were labelled with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI), and fluorescence signal was verified to originate solely from intact fusion proteins via anti-GFP western blot.

Fluorescence imaging was conducted in wheat protoplasts and N. benthamiana epidermal cells transiently expressing EpTFIIAγ–GFP. To induce drought-stress-related or osmotic stress-related cellular responses, cells were treated with 10% (w/v) PEG8000, 1.5 M sorbitol, 50 μM ABA or 250 mM NaCl as indicated. Imaging was performed with an FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus). GFP fluorescence was excited at 488 nm and emission was captured at 491–535 nm. Image acquisition and processing were performed using FV31S-SW software.

Industry observers note that molecular dynamics of EpTFIIAγ–GFP condensates were characterized through FRAP assays. Selected condensates were photobleached using a 488-nm laser, and fluorescence recovery was monitored by timelapse imaging. Recovery curves were normalized to both pre-bleach intensity and the fluorescence of adjacent unbleached regions to correct for background photobleaching; data were analysed with FV31S-SW software. Molecular mobility of EpTFIIAγ and the IDR deletion variant was assessed by FCS analysis in wheat protoplasts. Autocorrelation curves were acquired from multiple cells and fitted to appropriate diffusion models using CorTector NanoX FCS software to obtain diffusion coefficients and molecular concentrations.

To identify proteins that can potentially physically interact with EpTFIIAγ, a yeast two-hybrid screen was performed. The full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ was cloned into the pGBKT7 vector and served as the bait construct, fused to the binding domain of GAL4. The resulting pGBKT7-EpTFIIAγ plasmid was co-transformed with a pGADT7-based cDNA library (from wheat cv. Chinese Spring seedlings) into S. cerevisiae strain AH109 using the lithium acetate method, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Clontech). Positive clones were selected on selective dropout media, and candidate-interacting proteins were identified by PCR amplification and subsequent DNA sequencing.

It has been revealed that to validate putative physical interactions between EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ with candidate partners, the coding sequences lacking translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were individually cloned into the pGADT7 vector to form prey constructs. The coding sequences of EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were used as bait in the pGBKT7 vector. Bait and prey constructs were co-transformed into S. cerevisiae AH109 using the lithium-acetate method. Protein–protein interactions were assessed by spotting serial tenfold dilutions of co-transformed yeast cultures onto SD/–Trp–Leu and SD/–Trp–Leu–His–Ade selective media.

To perform luciferase-complementation imaging assays, the coding sequences of TaWRKY46, TaARF6, TaAKS1, TaVOZ1, TaTFIIAαβ and AtTFIIAαβ were cloned upstream of the nLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-nLUC vector, whereas EpTFIIAγ, EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR), TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were cloned downstream of the cLUC in the pCAMBIA1300-cLUC vector. These constructs were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and cultured overnight. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to an OD600 nm of 0.6 in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 150 μM acetosyringone and 10 mM MES, pH 5.6). Equal volumes of Agrobacteria carrying pairs of nLUC and cLUC constructs of interest and controls were co-infiltrated into 4-week-old N. benthamiana leaves. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, 150 μg ml−1 D-luciferin potassium salt (ST196, Beyotime) was sprayed onto the abaxial surface of tobacco leaves, followed by a 3-min dark reaction. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using a PlantView100 multispectral dynamic fluorescence microscope system (BLT Photon Technology).

For bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays, the full-length coding sequence of EpTFIIAγ lacking the translational stop codon was amplified and cloned into the cYFP vector pSm35s-cYFP (BioRun), whereas the coding sequences lacking the translational stop codons of TaAKS1, TaWRKY46, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 were amplified and cloned into the nYFP vector pSm35s-nYFP (BioRun). The resulting constructs were introduced into A. tumefaciens GV3101 and subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants. The infiltration buffer contained 10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, adjusted to pH 5.6. The bacterial suspension was diluted to an OD600 nm of 0.4 before infiltration. Forty-eight hours post-infiltration, YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) with an excitation wavelength of 514 nm and an emission wavelength range of 525–555 nm.

Sources indicate that the same constructs were transformed into wheat protoplasts, which were incubated for 20 h to allow transient expression. YFP signals were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus), with nuclei labelled using DAPI. Total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were obtained for SDS–PAGE and western blotting. Western blotting (described below) was performed using the primary antibody anti-GFP tag mouse monoclonal antibody (1:1,000; A02020, Abbkine), followed by horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibody (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

Full-length cDNAs of EpTFIIAγ, TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46 were amplified by PCR and cloned into the pMAL-c5X vector (for MBP tagging), pET32a (Novagen; for His or HA tagging) or the pGEX4T-1 vector (Merck; for GST-tagged expression) using the ClonExpress II One-Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme) following the manufacturers’ instructions and lacking the respective translational start or stop codons as required. The resulting recombinant plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli Rosetta and cultured in LB medium supplemented with ampicillin at 37 °C. When the culture reached OD600 nm of 0.4–0.6, protein expression was induced by adding 0.5 mM isopropyl-β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation at 16 °C for 14–16 h. The expressed proteins and corresponding controls were subsequently purified using the GST-tag Protein Purification Kit (P2253, Beyotime), anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) or Dextrin beads 6FF (SA026100, Smart-Lifesciences) according to the respective manufacturer’s protocols. The proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected with anti-HA (AH158-IgG1, Beyotime), anti-GST (AM926, Beyotime) and anti-MBP (66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group) antibodies, respectively.

In a recent development, MBP-tagged EpTFIIAγ, TaTFIIAγ and AtTFIIAγ were individually incubated with GST, GST–TaAKS1, GST–TaWRKY46, GST–TaARF6, HA–TaVOZ1, GST–TaTFIIAαβ or GST–AtTFIIAαβ at 4 °C for 3 h. Protein complexes were immunoprecipitated using BeyoGold GST-tag purification resin (P2253, Beyotime) or anti-HA affinity gel (P2287, Beyotime) at 4 °C for 4 h. After incubation, complexes were collected by centrifugation at 300g for 5 min, followed by five washes with phosphate-buffered saline. Proteins were separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and detected by western blotting (described below) using anti-GST antibody (1:1,000 dilution; AM926, Beyotime), anti-HA antibody (1:1,000 dilution, AF2305, Beyotime) and anti-MBP antibody (1:1,000 dilution; 66003-1-Ig, Proteintech Group), and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H + L) or goat anti-rabbit IgG (H + L) secondary antibodies (diluted 1:1,000; A0216 and A0208, respectively, Beyotime).

According to recent reports, for co-immunoprecipitation assays, fusion constructs including EpTFIIAγ–GFP, TaAKS1–GFP, TaARF6–mCherry, TaWRKY46–mCherry, EpTFIIAγ–mCherry and TaVOZ1–GFP were prepared in pCAMBIA1302 and pICH86988 vectors, respectively. Combinations of these constructs were co-transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101, which was subsequently infiltrated into the leaves of N. benthamiana in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid and 150 μM acetosyringone, pH of 5.6). After 48 h of transient expression, total proteins were extracted using RIPA complete lysis buffer (P1015, Beyotime) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail for plant cell and tissue extracts (P0040, Beyotime). The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000g for 15 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants were incubated with GFP-Trap beads (GTA-20, ChromoTek) at 4 °C for 3 h with gentle rotation. Corresponding protein complexes were obtained after a series of washing steps and elution steps. Input and eluted proteins were then resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Western blotting was performed using primary antibodies to GFP (1:2,000; AE012, Abclonal) or mCherry (1:1,000; ABM40125, Abbkine), followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500; P0946, Beyotime).

EpTFIIAγ and SEUSS69 were cloned into the pET-15b expression vector (for His tagging) and heterologously expressed in E. coli Rosetta cells. The recombinant proteins were purified using NTA-Ni magnetic agarose beads with the His-Tag Protein Purification Kit (P2247S, Beyotime) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For phase-separation assays, purified proteins were diluted to 10 μM in phase-separation buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM dithiothreitol). 10% PEG8000 was included as a molecular crowding agent to promote condensate formation. Samples were gently mixed and equilibrated at room temperature before imaging. Condensates were visualized using a FV3000 confocal laser-scanning microscope (Olympus) equipped with a ×60 oil-immersion objective (NA = 1.42) and images were processed using FV31S-SW software.

In a recent development, protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay kit (PA115-02, Tiangen Biotech). SDS–PAGE was performed with a PAGE Gel Fast Preparation Kit (EpiZyme). Protein samples (obtained from either prokaryotic expression, in vitro and in planta validation) were mixed with 5× SDS loading buffer at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. Ten micrograms of protein sample and 5 μl of 10–180 kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) were loaded onto gels. Electrophoresis was run at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. For wet transfer, the gel, 0.45-μm PVDF membrane and filter papers were soaked in transfer buffer (PS109, EpiZyme) for 15 min to equilibrate. A transfer stack was assembled, and transfer was conducted at a constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C. Post-transfer, the PVDF membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in transfer buffer; PS109, EpiZyme) on a shaker at room temperature for 2 h. The membrane was then incubated with primary antibody (1:1,000 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk, adjusted per antibody instructions) on a shaker at 4 °C overnight. After three washes with TBST (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl and 0.1% (v/v) Tween-20), the membrane was incubated with 1:1,000 HRP-labelled secondary antibody (diluted in 5% w/v non-fat milk) at room temperature for 1.5 h. The membrane was washed three times with TBST and once with TBS for 5 min. Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL substrate (34098CN, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after 2 min of dark incubation, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system.

Transgenic wheat, rice, maize and Arabidopsis plants, along with non-transgenic controls, were used for the assay for EpTFIIAγ abundance. The anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody was generated by Genecreate via rabbit immunization with EpTFIIAγ-specific short polypeptides, and its specificity was verified by western blotting. Seedlings of rice, maize and wheat were grown to the three-leaf stage under the aforementioned culture conditions; Arabidopsis seedlings were grown for 2 weeks. For each plant, 2 g of leaves were weighed, quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into powder in a pre-cooled mortar. The powder was transferred to a pre-cooled 50-ml centrifuge tube, and 5 ml of plant RIPA lysis buffer (P0045, Beyotime) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (50×; P1055, Beyotime) was added. After resuspension, the mixture was incubated on ice for 30 min, then centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected for subsequent experiments. Protein concentration was determined by the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) method. A total of 15–20 μg of protein was mixed with 5× SDS–PAGE sample loading buffer (P0015, Beyotime) at a 4:1 ratio, boiled at 95 °C for 5 min and cooled on ice. SDS–PAGE was performed with a 12% separating gel: electrophoresis at 80 V until samples entered the separating gel, then adjusted to 120 V until bromophenol blue reached the gel bottom. A 10–180-kDa molecular-weight marker (WJ103, EpiZyme) was used as a reference. Proteins were transferred to a 0.45-μm PVDF membrane by wet transfer (constant current of 300 mA at 4 °C for 90 min). The membrane was blocked with 5% w/v non-fat milk (prepared in TBST) at room temperature for 2 h, then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the anti-EpTFIIAγ antibody (1:500 dilution in 5% w/v non-fat milk). After three washes with TBST, the membrane was incubated with HRP-labelled goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (A0208, Beyotime) at 1:5,000 dilution for 1 h at room temperature. Following three additional TBST washes, the membrane was developed with ECL chemiluminescent substrate, and images were captured with a chemiluminescent imaging system. The target protein expression level was analysed based on the presence of the target band. Actin was used as a loading control, detected with an anti-actin antibody (AA128, Beyotime) and HRP-labelled goat anti-mouse secondary antibody (A0216, Beyotime).

Total protein was extracted from seedling leaves using plant protein extraction buffer (AS08300, Agrisera). Equal amounts of protein (10 μg) were resolved by 12.5% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Amersham, GE Healthcare). Membranes were probed with primary antibodies to Cyt b6 (AS184069, Agrisera), PsbA (AS05084, Agrisera), PsbD (AS06146, Agrisera), AtpB (AS05085, Agrisera), RbcL (AS03037, Agrisera), RbcS (AS07259, Agrisera), Lhca2 (AS01006, Agrisera) and Lhcb2 (AS01003, Agrisera) at the recommended dilutions, followed by incubation with a goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (1:10,000; AS09602, Agrisera). Actin (AA128, Beyotime) served as the loading control, and protein signals were visualized using the standard chemiluminescence detection described above.

Industry observers note that three-leaf-stage seedling leaves of transgenic wheat expressing EpTFIIAγ–HA in the cv. Fielder background were collected and used for ChIP as previously described70. In brief, 2 g of plant tissue was washed twice with cold phosphate-buffered saline buffer and crosslinked with 1% v/v formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature. The crosslinking was quenched by adding glycine to a final concentration of 125 mM. Samples were then lysed in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 10 mM EDTA, 1% w/v SDS and protease inhibitor cocktail. Chromatin was extracted on ice and sonicated to obtain soluble, sheared fragments with an average DNA length of 200–500 bp. A 20-μl aliquot was reserved as the input control and stored at –20 °C, whereas 100 μl of the sheared chromatin was used for immunoprecipitation with 10 μg of anti-HA antibody (ChIP grade, ab9110, Abcam) overnight at 4 °C. Subsequently, 30 μl of protein A/G magnetic beads was added, followed by incubation for 3 h. Beads were sequentially washed with low-salt buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 50 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% v/v Triton X-100 and 0.1% w/v SDS), twice with high-salt buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.1, 250 mM LiCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% v/v NP-40 and 1% w/v deoxycholic acid), and twice with TE buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 1 mM EDTA). Chromatin was eluted in 300 μl of elution buffer (100 mM NaHCO3 and 1% w/v SDS), treated with RNase A (8 μg ml−1) at 65 °C for 6 h, followed by proteinase K (345 μg ml−1) digestion overnight at 45 °C. Immunoprecipitated DNA was then used to prepare sequencing libraries using the NEXTFLEX ChIP–seq Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NOVA-5143-02, Bioo Scientific) and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using a paired-end 150-bp strategy.

In a recent development, low-quality sequencing reads were filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome (IWGSC RefSeq v1.1) using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72. SAMtools (v1.3.1)73 was used to remove PCR duplicates from the aligned data. MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 was used for peak calling using default parameters (bandwidth = 300 bp; model fold = 5, 50; q value = 0.05). Each peak was assigned to the gene for the TSS of which was closest to the peak midpoint. Motif analysis within the peaks was conducted using HOMER (v3)75 with default settings and a maximum motif length of 12 bp. Gene Ontology functional enrichment analysis was performed using the clusterProfiler package in R76. Statistical significance was determined using a hypergeometric test with a P value threshold of 0.05.

To validate ChIP–seq results, ChIP–qPCR was performed. One microlitre of purified ChIP DNA was used as template in a 20-μl qPCR containing SYBR Green Master Mix (Q121-02/03, Vazyme). Amplification was carried out using a Bio-Rad CFX96 real-time PCR system. Primers were designed to amplify genomic regions containing predicted binding sites based on ChIP–seq results. Each qPCR was conducted in four times. Enrichment values were calculated as mean ± s.d. from three biological replicates and are presented. Non-specific IgG and primers targeting intergenic regions were included as negative controls. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 15.

Total RNA was extracted from leaves of wild-type Fielder and two EpTFIIAγ–HA transgenic lines (TL4 and TL7) using TRIzol reagent (15596026, Invitrogen). Genomic DNA was removed by DNase I treatment following extraction. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a Nanodrop OneC Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) by examining the A260:A280 ratio. RNA integrity was confirmed through 1.5% w/v agarose gel electrophoresis and quantified using a Qubit 3.0 fluorometer with the Qubit RNA Broad Range Assay kit (Q10210, Life Technologies). For library construction, 2 μg of total RNA was used to prepare strand-specific RNA-seq libraries with the KC Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (DR08402, Wuhan Seqhealth), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were enriched for fragments ranging from 200 to 500 bp, quantified and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform using paired-end reads.

Recent findings suggest that raw sequencing reads were quality filtered using Trimmomatic (v0.36)71 to remove adapter sequences and low-quality reads. Clean reads were aligned to the wheat reference genome IWGSC RefSeq (v1.1) using GEM (v2.5)77. PCR duplicates were removed, and gene expression levels were quantified using DESeq2 (ref. 78). DEGs were identified using a threshold of |log2 (fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. Gene Ontology classification and enrichment analysis of DEGs were conducted using the clusterProfiler package76, identifying statistically significantly enriched terms among upregulated and downregulated genes.

Paired-end CUT&Tag79 reads were quality filtered with fastp80 and aligned to the wheat cv. Fielder reference genome using bowtie2 (v2.5.4)72 in end-to-end, very-sensitive mode. Reads with mapping quality < 20 were removed, and duplicate reads were removed after processing with samtools fixmate and samtools markdup73. Genome-wide RPKM-normalized bigWig tracks were generated with deepTools bamCoverage, and signal enrichment around genes and TSSs was visualized using computeMatrix and plotHeatmap81. Peaks were called for each replicate with MACS3 (v3.0.3)74 using matched IgG/input controls. Reproducible peaks between biological replicates were identified using IDR82 and used as consensus peaks. Consensus peaks were annotated against the Fielder genome annotation83. Promoter-associated target genes were defined at the peak–gene pair level: a gene was retained only when its own signed distance from the peak to the TSS satisfied distance to TSS ≤ 3 kb. Motif enrichment was performed on promoter peak regions using HOMER75 with sequence extraction and shuffled genomic background generation performed using BEDTools84.

Recent findings suggest that EMSA was performed using the Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (GS009, Beyotime Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Biotin-labelled DNA probes containing putative binding motifs were synthesized by Sangon Biotech and used at a final concentration of 0.05 μM per reaction. Each 20-μl binding reaction contained 4 μl of 5× EMSA/gel-shift binding buffer, 1 μg of recombinant protein (MBP tagged or GST tagged) and the biotin-labelled probe. Reactions were incubated at 23 °C for 30 min, then separated on a native 8% polyacrylamide gel in 0.5× TBE buffer (R0223, Beyontime) at 100 V for 1 h. DNA–protein complexes were transferred onto a nylon membrane (FFN10, Beyontime) and crosslinked by UV. Detection of biotin-labelled DNA was performed using a streptavidin–HRP conjugate and chemiluminescent substrate according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Negative controls included using MBP or GST. Washing and visualization were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

To assess transcriptional regulation mediated by EpTFIIAγ, 1.5-kb promoter regions of selected target genes were cloned into the pGreenII-0800-LUC vector to produce reporter constructs, whereas the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector to produce an effector construct25. Empty pGreenII-0800-LUC and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. LUC and REN activities were subsequently measured using the Dual Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit (RG027, Beyotime), and relative luciferase activity was calculated as the ratio of LUC-to-REN activity.

According to recent reports, to investigate the effect of EpTFIIAγ on the transcriptional activity of its assayed interacting proteins (TaAKS1, TaARF6, TaVOZ1 and TaWRKY46), the EpTFIIAγ coding sequence was cloned into the pCAMBIA1302 vector, whereas the coding sequences of the transcription factors were cloned into the pGreenII-62-SK vector. Promoter regions (1.5 kb) of downstream target genes (TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1) were cloned into pGreenII-0800-LUC to generate reporter constructs. Effector and reporter plasmids were transformed into A. tumefaciens GV3101 (pSoup-p19), which was subsequently co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves and left to allow transient expression for 2 days. Luciferase activities were measured as described above, and relative transcriptional activity was determined by calculating the LUC:REN ratio. Empty pCAMBIA1302 and pGreenII-62-SK vectors were used as negative controls. All experiments were conducted with at least three biological replicates.

Fungal and plant TFIIAγ candidates were retrieved from the JGI MycoCosm portal85 and the OneKP project86, respectively. Protein-level similarity searches were conducted using EpTFIIAγ and representative TFIIAγ proteins as queries. Partial fragments and sequences with abnormal lengths (outside 70–150 amino acids) were removed. Redundant identical sequences from the same species were collapsed, but distinct isoforms passing the filtering criteria were retained. Ultimately, 3,183 fungal and 1,245 Viridiplantae sequences were included, resulting in a final dataset of 4,428 TFIIAγ proteins (Supplementary Table 7).

It has been revealed that filtered protein sequences were aligned with MAFFT (v7.525)87 using the automatic strategy selection mode. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic inference was performed with IQ-TREE (v3.0.1)88. The best-fitting amino acid substitution model was selected with ModelFinder, and branch support was estimated using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates and 1,000 Shimodaira–Hasegawa-like approximate likelihood ratio test replicates. The resulting tree was visualized as a circular phylogeny using custom Python scripts with Biopython (v1.84) and Matplotlib (v3.10.8).

Protein structure prediction for TFIIAγ was conducted using AlphaFold3 (ref. 89) for orthologues from E. pusillum (EPUS02736), wheat (TraesCS1D02G024600), rice (LOC_Os01g73890), maize (Zm00001eb356100) and Arabidopsis (AT4G24440) with default parameters, and the resulting models were visualized using PyMOL (v3.1.0).

Statistical tests were conducted using two-tailed Student’s t-tests, Kruskal–Wallis tests, one-way ANOVA, and Brown-Forsythe and Welch ANOVA in GraphPad Prism (v9.5.0). Differences were considered statistically significant at *P < 0.05 or **P < 0.01. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. from at least three independent biological replicates or independent experiments unless otherwise specified in legends.

J.W., Z.K. and H.M. conceived the original idea and designed the early experiments. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the major experimental work. Specifically, L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.W., P.J., Y.H., D.T., S.Y., Q.W., S.T., Z.S., L.S., M.Y., T.X., Y.L., S.Z., P.Z., W.F., J.H., J.Z. and G.Z. contributed to plant cultivation and phenotypic characterization under controlled and field conditions, including stress-resistance phenotyping, agronomic trait assessment, grain-filling analysis and physiological measurements. X.H. generated the transgenic plants. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.F., C.W., B.L., S.T., Z.S., L.S. and J.H. conducted the microscopy and imaging analyses. F.L., H.Z., B.L., C.W., D.T. and Q.W. performed the biochemical and protein-related experiments. L.D., F.L., H.Z., C.W., S.W., S.L. and D.T. conducted the molecular and transcriptional regulation assays. B.C., Z.Q. and Y.W. performed the genomic, transcriptomic and computational analyses. L.D. and Z.Q. conducted the phylogenetic analysis and protein structure prediction. L.D., F.L., X.Q., H.Z., C.F. and C.W. performed the statistical analyses and data quantification. H.M. and L.D. wrote the manuscript with input from X.Q., J.W. and Z.K. All authors reviewed and approved the final manuscript.

In a recent development, A patent application related to the work described in this article has been filed in China. The patent applicants are the Institute of Microbiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences and Northwest A&F University. The inventors are J.W., Z.K., X.Q., H.M., Xinli Wei, Y.W. and F.L. The application number is 202111602359.2, and the patent application is at the moment under substantive examination. The patent application covers the use of the extremophile gene EpTFIIAγ for improving abiotic stress resistance in wheat, rice and maize. The other authors declare no other competing interests.

It has been revealed that (a) Functional co-expression network of EpTFIIAγ target genes. Co-expression relationships among EpTFIIAγ target genes were inferred from published expression data (https://wheat.cau.edu.cn/wGRN/) using the WGCNA signed topological overlap matrix (TOM). Node color denotes functional module, and larger nodes indicate EMSA-validated targets. (b, c) Volcano plots showing up-regulated and down-regulated genes in transgenic EpTFIIAγ line 4 (b) and line 7 (c) versus wild-type Fielder under well-watered conditions. Transcripts with a fold change > 2 or < 0.5 and an adjusted P-value < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. (d, e) Venn diagram of up-regulated (d) and down-regulated (e) differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in two transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines compared to Fielder controls (|Fold Change| > 2, P < 0.05). (f, g) Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of up-regulated (f) and down-regulated (g) genes identified in transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines. In (b-e), statistical analysis of differentially expressed genes was conducted using the two-sided Wald test within the DESeq2 R package, with subsequent adjustment for multiple comparisons achieved through the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method. In (f) and (g), statistical analysis was assessed using a one-sided hypergeometric over-representation test.

There’s been a lot noted about Francesco Camarda’s future in recent months and it seems AC Milan are getting closer to a decision.

Industry observers note that put simply, Milan are in the same situation that they were a few years ago. Camarda isn’t playing and when he does, he’s not really getting the most out of games. So, another loan will be sought in the mercato.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Recent findings suggest that his time with Lecce previously wasn’t exactly fruitful, but he did grab a first Serie A goal, which helped. However, he’s still without a competitive goal for the Rossoneri and his minutes aren’t regular. In other words, it’s looking like another six months wasted.

So, he’ll leave the nest in January once again.

Talk of a move abroad has been really common recently, and it seems increasingly likely that his next test will be abroad. However, there are no inklings about where it may be, even in Matteo Moretto’s latest patch on Fabrizio Romano’s YouTube channel, as MilanNews relays.

“AC Milan ‘s decision has essentially already been made: they want the boy to be able to play consistently and consistently, trying a different experience.

“There’s been a lot of talk about Cagliari, there’s been a lot of talk about Genoa, there’s been a lot of talk about Italy, but as I’ve remarked in recent days, keep an eye on options that lead abroad.

In a recent development, “It’s true that there are Italian teams interested in Camarda, but as of today, I can’t see Genoa and Cagliari pursuing the player, despite preliminary discussions. Cagliari, in particular, had inquired about the terms, but nothing more and nothing less.

Recent findings suggest that “This solution, from what I understand, is unlikely to go ahead. I might keep a small door open to Italy for you, but the real door is a door that leads abroad.

“Keep an eye on foreign championships, keep an eye on championships and teams that give confidence to young people, that let young people play and that give young people space. So, as of today, this is the line on Camarda.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the club’s decision to go for a change at the top has caused a huge amount of upset – with many fans saying it is a shocking decision and a number of Macdonald’s squad deciding to follow him out of the door. And it is the way the decision appears to have been handled that has caused the most anger.

As the week unfolded, Town – who are second from bottom of the Isthmian South East division after only two wins in 19 games – appointed club stalwart Dave Winterton as interim manager, with senior player Arron Hopkinson assisting him, and asked fans to get behind him.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

And they put out an advert inviting applicants for the job, with talk of them wanting to take the whole club – not just the men’s first team – forward as one.

Macdonald’s right-hand man Ben Davis has gone in the wake of the sacking and so, reportedly, have long-serving Adam Davidson and at least five players.

Macdonald gave an exclusive interview to the Eastbourne Herald and sussexworld.co.uk in which he said he had been told eight days before he was sacked that his job was ‘bomb-proof’ all the time the chairman was in place.

He also mentioned he had learned the club had decided they wanted a change of manager on November 16 – and only after two more games, training and two more siginings did they tell him. Macdonald told us he was asked if would resign, but refused.

You can read our full interview with Macdonald, who has been at the helm since 2022, on pages 62 & 63. He finished it with these words: “You don’t often get the chance to manage the club from the town you grew up in and I’ve just committed over 10% of my life to it, so the next few days and weeks will just be reflecting on that and appreciating the opportunity that the club gave me four-and-a-half years ago, and the continued and consistent success we have given them in return.”.

As for what happens next, Winterton isinterim manager and the Town committee have asked fans to get behind him as he guides the squad through what will be a tricky period.

The immediate aim is to try to get out of the Isthmian SE danger zone, and that starts with a visit to Erith Town tomorrow, followed by a home Sussex derby with Broadbridge Heath a week later.

Those won’t be easy games with a number of Macdonald’s players announcing they also left – including James Waters, who had only rejoined the club a day before the manager was ousted.

According to recent reports, meanwhile the club – who gave ‘sincere thanks’ to Macdonald in their statement revealing he was leaving – are inviting applicants for the vacancy. They said: “We are looking for an individual who shares our ambition, understands the importance of building a strong club culture and is passionate about developing players, creating opportunities and delivering success both on and off the pitch.

"At Eastbourne Town, we believe the First Team should be an vital part of a wider football development pathway. We want to create an environment where young players can see a realistic route from youth football through U18 and U23 football and ultimately into the first team.”.

Read the stories from Town’s turbulent week in today’s Eastbourne Herald.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since taking over, the Reds are unbeaten in four in the league, and despite dropping out of both cup competitions in the space of three days, there has been a mentality shift in the players – and the fans have seen that the players are giving their all.

Despite Christmas just being around the corner, the club hope Reds fans travel in their numbers to Exter to cheer the boys on in an early kick off. But it has been noted that Blackwell doesn’t celebrate with the players like past managers have.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Speaking in his pre-Exeter press conference, Blackwell remarked one or two fans asked him why he didn’t go and thank the support: “I thank the fans all the time, but after the game, it’s important that the players get the credit, not the manager.

“That’s not my job. My job is to try to prepare the team, and the players go out and give everything. If they do that, that’s what the fans want. They don’t want me walking up and down the pitch clapping and whatever. Get on, do your job Blackwell, do your job. And if that’s the case, the players are doing well.”.

Recent findings suggest that he added: “It’s not my style. I enjoy them enjoying it and I enjoy that the fans enjoy it. I’ve had a great career, managing massive clubs and been a long way in big competitions, been all over the world, and I’ve never wanted the adulation.

“I just enjoy other people having it and seeing my players get that and the fans enjoying it. Sending them home after a week’s work, seeing the players give everything. That’s what they want. If we can keep doing that, I think we keep them on-side.”.

Talking about the bond between players and fans, Blackwell said “I want the players to take the credit because the bond is between the players and the fans, and that’s the bond.

"As an ex-player, I knew there was a great bond between me and the fans. I’d hate to think that the manager walked up and started taking my thunder after having a man of the match performance and he walks up and takes all the credit. No, I want the players to have the credit.”.

Looking to remain top of the League One table heading into the final month of the year, Stockport County welcome Leyton Orient to Edgeley Park on Saturday afternoon.

The Hatters currently hold a three-point lead at the summit after recording their third consecutive victory with a 3-0 win away to Cambridge United, while the O's are hoping to close the gap on the playoff places after beating AFC Wimbledon 4-1 last time out.

Following their agonisingly narrow failure to secure promotion to the Championship last season, Stockport County parted ways with long-serving manager Dave Challinor and appointed former Rochdale boss Jimmy McNulty as his replacement.

McNulty has so far overseen 21 matches in charge of the Hatters across all competitions, recording 13 wins, four draws and four defeats to give him an impressive win rate of 61.9%.

Ten of those victories have come in League One, with Stockport looking to enter December at the top of the table after collecting 32 points from their opening 16 matches, a lead they could extend to six points if results elsewhere go their way and they secure a fourth consecutive league win.

Their impressive league form has also carried over into the cup competitions, with McNulty's men finishing top of their EFL Trophy group and booking their place in the next round of the FA Cup, although they survived a major scare earlier this month, coming from two goals behind to beat Isthmian League side Cray Wanderers 3-2.

More recently, the Greater Manchester outfit climbed to the summit of League One with an emphatic 3-0 victory over Cambridge, a match that featured a superb free-kick from captain Oliver Norwood.

The three goals scored last weekend took Stockport's league tally to 32 for the season, a total bettered by no other side in the third tier and only three teams across England's top four divisions.

As for visitors Leyton Orient, they have enjoyed a more consistent campaign this time around after spending much of the 2025-26 season battling near the bottom of the table and ultimately finishing just one place above the relegation zone.

After their opening 14 League One matches, the London-based side sit 12th under the continued leadership of Richie Wellens, who recently surpassed 250 games in charge of the O's, with six wins, two draws and six defeats leaving them on 20 points.

Although victory on Saturday, at a ground where Stockport boast the best home record in the division, would not be enough to lift Orient into the playoff places, it could leave them just three points outside the top six, with games in hand over all but one of the teams at the moment above them.

The O's most recently continued their impressive home form with a convincing 4-1 victory over London neighbours AFC Wimbledon, securing their fourth league win in their last five matches at Brisbane Road.

In fact, Wellens' side are already closing in on surpassing their total number of home victories from the whole of last season, having won half of their league fixtures on home soil so far in 2026-27.

Although the two sides finished at opposite ends of the table last season, neither could claim bragging rights in their meetings, with both encounters ending in draws.

The last time either side won this fixture within 90 minutes was in February 2025, the same season they faced each other in the League One playoff semi-finals.

Leyton Orient also look set to travel from the capital with the option of naming an unchanged starting XI following last weekend's victory.

And Washington, as part of his weekly EFL column for BestBettingBonuses.co.uk, said owners need to be honest and transparent, especially when things aren’t going well.

The 21-year-old has been limited to 41 minutes of top-flight action across four substitute appearances this season after being loaned to Feyenoord, Auxerre and Birmingham since his 2024 arrival from Danish club Nordsjaelland.

“It’s not always the fact that he has to do more; sometimes the players who are right now on the pitch do a lot to stay on the pitch,” said Hurzeler.

“Therefore he needs to keep working hard, he needs to be patient, he needs to be there when we need him.

“We have plenty of games in the next weeks and I always emphasise that we need the full squad, that we need everyone, everyone will play an important role for us.

“No matter how many minutes you play, you need to contribute to the success for this club and we need to always put the team first. Some players might have to be a little bit more patient but in the right moment you need to be there so you have to always be ready and alive to support the team.”.

By Darren Plant | 26 Nov 2026 15:13.

Xabi Alonso has revealed that Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana has apologised for comments made in an interview earlier this week.

The Blues are at the moment preparing for a Premier League fixture against Nottingham Forest on Friday night.

Sitting in eighth place in the Premier League table after three defeats in four matches, Alonso could have done without any controversy away from the pitch.

Instead, Fofana gave an interview where he revealed that he considered retirement during a prolonged spell on the sidelines with serious knee injuries.

Not only did the Frenchman add that he was convinced to continue playing by his agent because of the money he could earn, Fofana hinted that he was not overly disappointed to miss a spot kick in a penalty shootout against Liverpool last month.

Addressing the situation at a press conference, Alonso suggested that he had been left furious by Fofana's words.

He told reporters: "Absolutely, we have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate.

"He apologised, he knows it was not right the moment, it was not right the content, we are here to take things seriously and he said that it's not going to be repeated and we know that it's something that we don't want, these kind of things and they are not going to be repeated for sure.".

The Spaniard added that he now regarded the matter as "closed", indicating that Fofana remains available to face Forest.

Fofana's place in the Chelsea defence had already been in doubt due to the level of his performance in the 4-1 defeat versus Leeds last weekend.

Although there have been games this season where the 25-year-old has played to an acceptable standard, his attitude and decision-making in the Chelsea backline has been questioned for months.

Maxence Lacroix's hamstring injury has led to Fofana partnering Levi Colwill, but they have performed poorly both individually and as a partnership.

Alonso may consider using Josh Acheampong alongside Colwill versus Forest, but that could potentially cause concerns at full-back.

Brighton still require six more points to guarantee their place in the last 16 of the Uefa Conference League following Thursday night's impressive 4-0 victory over Romanian league leaders Craiova.

Fabian Hurzeler's side are currently second in the league phase table - behind leaders Monaco - with 10 points from their opening four matches, putting them in a strong position to secure automatic qualification for the knockout stages.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The top eight teams qualify directly for the last 16, while those finishing between ninth and 24th must negotiate an additional knockout play-off round.

Brighton have two league-phase fixtures remaining, starting with a home meeting against leaders Monaco on December 10 before travelling to face Panathinaikos on December 17.

Winning both matches would take the Seagulls to 16 points and guarantee a top-eight finish, regardless of results elsewhere.

Four points from the remaining games would leave them on 14 and extremely well placed, although mathematical qualification would not be certain.

Three points would see them to 13 points and would still have a strong chance, depending on other results.

Hurzeler will be particularly encouraged by Brighton's defensive record, with the Seagulls yet to concede a goal in their four Conference League matches.

The Albion have scored nine times and will now look to finish the league phase strongly and avoid the extra play-off round in February.

Head coach Fabian Hurzeler was delighted with the performance against Craiova.

The German said: “I think that was a really good start, and also very vital to make the game look easy, because especially the first goal helped us force [the opponent] to open up the space,” he said.

Sources indicate that “That meant we could have more space to combine and more opportunity to attack their box. So I think we were very professional with good standards in the first half. Then, of course, the red card definitely helped us to finish - or to change - the structure of the game.

“In the second half we created plenty of chances. I wasn't happy that we weren't clinical and clean enough finishing these chances, because I think we dropped our level a little bit there. Overall, though, winning 4–0 means that we did a lot of things well.”.

Here are the key dates for the 2026/27 UEFA Conference League knockout stages, should Brighton progress:.

- Knockout play-off round: February 18 and 25, 2027.

- Round of 16: March 11 and 18, 2027.

- Quarter-finals: April 8 and 15, 2027.

- Semi-finals: April 29 and May 6, 2027.

- Final: June 2, 2027 – Beşiktaş Stadium, Istanbul, Turkey.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) firm.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Sources indicate that nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It noted in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.".

In a recent development, "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company remarked Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.".

The organization's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

According to recent reports, "He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine.".

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a tech giant remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

Recent findings suggest that "His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this.".

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, noted the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he noted.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the manufacturer is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO.".

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

Sources indicate that however, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Industry observers note that windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he mentioned.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

Sources indicate that however, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

Recent findings suggest that hürzeler insists he is happy with the attacking options already at his disposal, pointing to Brighton’s goalscoring record and the number of players capable of finding the net. Albion lead the Premier League goals scored table, finding the net 26 times in 11 games.

Asked about Lineker and Shearer’s praise for Brighton as one of the most entertaining teams in the league, Hürzeler welcomed the recognition but stressed that performances, rather than outside opinion, must remain the priority.

“If they say this, of course we should listen to it,” he mentioned.

"We should appreciate the opinion.

“On the other side, being the best football team doesn't mean you automatically win games.

“The truth is always on the pitch, and therefore we have to get back to our highest level.”.

Hürzeler was more emphatic when asked whether he agreed with Lineker’s suggestion that Brighton were missing a clinical, traditional centre-forward.

“An Alan Shearer?” the German replied, tongue-in-cheek.

“No, no. I think we have a lot of good strikers. When you look at how many goals we've scored in the season so far, and how many goals we scored today.

"We might not have one striker but we have plenty of players who are able to score goals.

“That's what has made us strong in the past and what will make us strong in the future, hopefully on Sunday as well.”.

The Brighton head coach was speaking after his side responded to their disappointing 2-0 defeat at Hull City with a 4-0 victory over Craiova in the UEFA Conference League.

Next up is a home match against Newcastle United, in the Premier League, this weekend.

Hürzeler specifically named the attacking players he believes can provide the goals, making clear that he has no concerns about the options available to him.

In a recent development, he added: “We're very happy with Kostoulas. We're very happy with [Georginio] Rutter.

"We're also happy with Tobi [Promise David], who came onto the pitch today against Craiova.”.

The head coach also appeared keen to ensure that the defeat at Hull did not define the assessment of his team's attacking play.

Brighton created opportunities at the MKM Stadium but were unable to find a way past an inspired goalkeeper, in Konstantinos Tzolakis, prompting Lineker to suggest that a striker with Vardy's instincts could make them much harder to stop.

Hürzeler, however, would rather focus on the wider picture than one frustrating afternoon in front of goal.

“We're focusing on the positives,” he noted.

"We are not focusing on one game where we missed a few chances.”.

The 4-0 victory over Craiova offered an immediate reminder of Brighton's goalscoring capabilities, although Hürzeler will now want his players to carry that performance into Sunday's match.
